Tides happen because the ocean is pulled by gravity, most powerfully by the moon. As the moon orbits the Earth, its gravitational force tugs on our planet. Water is fluid and mobile, so it responds to this tug more dramatically than the solid ground beneath it. Where the moon is overhead, its pull draws the sea toward it, creating a bulge of water that we experience as high tide. On the opposite side of the Earth, a second bulge forms as well, not because the moon pulls water there directly, but because the Earth itself is pulled toward the moon, leaving water behind on the far side. 

As the Earth rotates beneath these two bulges, any given coastline passes through them once or twice a day, which is why most places see two high tides and two low tides in each twenty-four hour period. The moon is not the only influence. The sun also exerts a gravitational pull on the oceans, though it is farther away and its effect
